{{Short description|Representation theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Plancherel theorem for spherical functions''' is an important result in the [[group representation|representation theory]] of [[semisimple Lie group]]s, due in its final form to [[Harish-Chandra]]. It is a natural generalisation in [[non-commutative harmonic analysis]] of the [[Plancherel formula]] and [[Fourier inversion formula]] in the representation theory of the group of real numbers in classical [[harmonic analysis]] and has a similarly close interconnection with the theory of [[differential equation]]s.
It is the special case for [[zonal spherical function]]s of the general [[Plancherel theorem]] for semisimple Lie groups, also proved by Harish-Chandra. The Plancherel theorem gives the [[Spectral theory|eigenfunction expansion]] of radial functions for the [[Laplacian operator]] on the associated [[symmetric space]] ''X''; it also gives the [[direct integral|direct integral decomposition]] into [[irreducible representation]]s of the [[regular representation]] on {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>(''X'')}}. In the case of [[hyperbolic space]], these expansions were known from [[Spectral theory of ordinary differential equations#Application to the hypergeometric equation|prior results]] of [[Gustav Ferdinand Mehler|Mehler]], [[Weyl]] and [[Vladimir Fock|Fock]].

The main reference for almost all this material is the encyclopedic text of {{harvtxt|Helgason|1984}}.

==History==
The first versions of an abstract Plancherel formula for the Fourier transform on a [[unimodular group|unimodular]] [[locally compact group]] ''G'' were due to Segal and Mautner.<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|pp=492–493}}, historical notes on the Plancherel theorem for spherical functions</ref> At around the same time, Harish-Chandra<ref>{{harvnb|Harish-Chandra|1951}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Harish-Chandra|1952}}</ref> and Gelfand & Naimark<ref>{{harvnb|Gelfand|Naimark|1948}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Guillemin|Sternberg|1977}}</ref> derived an explicit formula for [[SL(2,R)]] and complex [[semisimple Lie group]]s, so in particular the [[Lorentz group]]s. A simpler abstract formula was derived by Mautner for a "topological" symmetric space ''G''/''K'' corresponding to a [[maximal compact subgroup]] ''K''. [[Roger Godement|Godement]] gave a more concrete and satisfactory form for [[positive definite function on a group|positive definite]] [[zonal spherical function|spherical functions]], a class of [[special function]]s on ''G''/''K''. Since when ''G'' is a [[semisimple Lie group]] these spherical functions φ<sub>λ</sub> were naturally labelled by a parameter λ in the quotient of a [[Euclidean space]] by the action of a [[finite reflection group]], it became a central problem to determine explicitly the [[Plancherel measure]] in terms of this parametrization. Generalizing the ideas of [[Hermann Weyl]] from the [[spectral theory of ordinary differential equations]], Harish-Chandra<ref name="HarishChandra1958">{{harvnb|Harish-Chandra|1958a}}</ref><ref name="HarishChandra1958a">{{harvnb|Harish-Chandra|1958b}}</ref> introduced his celebrated '''c-function''' ''c''(λ) to describe the asymptotic behaviour of the spherical functions φ<sub>λ</sub> and proposed ''c''(λ)<sup>−2</sup> ''d''λ as the Plancherel measure. He verified this formula for the special cases when ''G'' is complex or [[Iwasawa decomposition|real rank]] one, thus in particular covering the case when ''G''/''K'' is a [[hyperbolic space]]. The general case was reduced to two conjectures about the properties of the c-function and the so-called spherical Fourier transform. Explicit formulas for the c-function were later obtained for a large class of classical semisimple Lie groups by Bhanu-Murthy. In turn these formulas prompted Gindikin and Karpelevich to derive a product formula<ref>{{harvnb|Gindikin|Karpelevich|1962}}</ref> for the c-function, reducing the computation to Harish-Chandra's formula for the rank 1 case. Their work finally enabled Harish-Chandra to complete his proof of the Plancherel theorem for spherical functions in 1966.<ref>{{harvnb|Harish-Chandra|1966}}, section 21</ref>

In many special cases, for example for complex [[Reductive group|semisimple group]] or the Lorentz groups, there are simple methods to develop the theory directly. Certain subgroups of these groups can be treated by techniques generalising the well-known "[[method of descent]]" due to [[Jacques Hadamard]]. In particular {{harvtxt|Flensted-Jensen|1978}} gave a general method for deducing properties of the spherical transform for a real semisimple group from that of its complexification.

One of the principal applications and motivations for the spherical transform was [[Selberg's trace formula]]. The classical [[Poisson summation formula]] combines the Fourier inversion formula on a vector group with summation over a cocompact lattice. In Selberg's analogue of this formula, the vector group is replaced by ''G''/''K'', the Fourier transform by the spherical transform and the lattice by a cocompact (or cofinite) [[Discrete group|discrete subgroup]]. The original paper of {{harvtxt|Selberg|1956}} implicitly invokes the spherical transform; it was {{harvtxt|Godement|1957}} who brought the transform to the fore, giving in particular an elementary treatment for SL(2,'''R''') along the lines sketched by Selberg.

==Spherical functions==
{{main article|Zonal spherical function}}
Let ''G'' be a [[semisimple Lie algebra|semisimple]] [[Lie group]] and ''K'' a [[maximal compact subgroup]] of ''G''. The [[Hecke algebra of a locally compact group|Hecke algebra]] ''C''<sub>c</sub>(''K'' \''G''/''K''), consisting of compactly supported ''K''-biinvariant continuous functions on ''G'', acts by convolution on the [[Hilbert space]] ''H''=''L''<sup>2</sup>(''G'' / ''K''). Because ''G'' / ''K'' is a [[symmetric space]], this *-algebra is [[commutative]]. The closure of its (the Hecke algebra's) image in the [[operator norm]] is a non-unital commutative [[C* algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{A}</math>, so by the [[Gelfand isomorphism]] can be identified with the continuous functions vanishing at infinity on its [[spectrum]] ''X''.<ref>The spectrum coincides with that of the commutative Banach *-algebra of integrable ''K''-biinvariant functions on ''G'' under convolution, a dense *-subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{A}</math>.</ref> Points in the spectrum are given by continuous *-homomorphisms of <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> into '''C''', i.e. [[Gelfand isomorphism|characters]] of <math>\mathfrak{A}</math>.

If ''S''' denotes the [[commutant]] of a set of operators ''S'' on ''H'', then <math>\mathfrak{A}^\prime</math> can be identified with the commutant of the [[regular representation]] of ''G'' on ''H''. Now <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> leaves invariant the subspace ''H''<sub>0</sub> of ''K''-invariant vectors in ''H''. Moreover, the [[abelian von Neumann algebra]] it generates on ''H''<sub>0</sub> is maximal Abelian. By [[spectral theory]], there is an essentially unique<ref>The [[Equivalence (measure theory)|measure class]] of μ in the sense of the [[Radon–Nikodym theorem]] is unique.</ref> [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] μ on the [[locally compact]] space ''X'' and a unitary transformation ''U'' between ''H''<sub>0</sub> and ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', μ) which carries the operators in <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> onto the corresponding [[multiplication operator]]s.

The transformation ''U'' is called the '''spherical Fourier transform''' or sometimes just the '''spherical transform''' and μ is called the '''[[Plancherel measure]]'''. The Hilbert space ''H''<sub>0</sub> can be identified with ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''K''\''G''/''K''), the space of ''K''-biinvariant square integrable functions on ''G''.

The characters χ<sub>λ</sub> of <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> (i.e. the points of ''X'') can be described by [[positive definite function on a group|positive definite]] [[zonal spherical function|spherical functions]] φ<sub>λ</sub> on ''G'', via the formula
<math display="block"> \chi_\lambda(\pi(f)) = \int_G f(g)\cdot \varphi_\lambda(g) \, dg.</math>
for ''f'' in ''C''<sub>c</sub>(''K''\''G''/''K''), where π(''f'') denotes the convolution operator in <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> and the integral is with respect to [[Haar measure]] on ''G''.

The spherical functions φ<sub>λ</sub> on ''G'' are given by [[Zonal spherical function#Harish-Chandra's formula|Harish-Chandra's formula]]:

:{| border="1" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="5"
|<math>\varphi_\lambda(g) = \int_K \lambda^\prime(gk)^{-1}\, dk. </math>
|}

In this formula:

* the integral is with respect to Haar measure on ''K'';
* λ is an element of ''A''* =Hom(''A'','''T''') where ''A'' is the Abelian vector subgroup in the [[Iwasawa decomposition]] ''G'' =''KAN'' of ''G'';
* λ' is defined on ''G'' by first extending λ to a [[character (mathematics)|character]] of the [[solvable group|solvable subgroup]] ''AN'', using the group homomorphism onto ''A'', and then setting <math display="block">\lambda'(kx) = \Delta_{AN}(x)^{1/2} \lambda(x)</math> for ''k'' in ''K'' and ''x'' in ''AN'', where Δ<sub>''AN''</sub> is the [[Haar measure#The modular function|modular function]] of ''AN''.
* Two different characters λ<sub>1</sub> and λ<sub>2</sub> give the same spherical function if and only if λ<sub>1</sub> = λ<sub>2</sub>·''s'', where ''s'' is in the [[Weyl group]] of ''A'' <math display="block"> W=N_K(A)/C_K(A),</math> the quotient of the [[normaliser]] of ''A'' in ''K'' by its [[centraliser]], a [[finite reflection group]].

It follows that

* '''''X'' can be identified with the quotient space ''A''*/''W'''''.

==Spherical principal series==
{{see also|Principal series representation}}
The spherical function φ<sub>λ</sub> can be identified with the matrix coefficient of the '''spherical principal series''' of ''G''. If ''M'' is the [[centraliser]] of ''A'' in ''K'', this is defined as the unitary representation π<sub>λ</sub> of ''G'' [[induced representation|induced]] by the character of ''B'' = ''MAN'' given by the composition of the homomorphism of ''MAN'' onto ''A'' and the character λ.
The induced representation is defined on functions ''f'' on ''G'' with
<math display="block"> f(gb)=\Delta(b)^{1/2} \lambda(b) f(g)</math>
for ''b'' in ''B'' by
<math display="block">\pi(g)f(x)=f(g^{-1}x),</math>
where
<math display="block"> \|f\|^2 = \int_K |f(k)|^2 \, dk < \infty.</math>

The functions ''f'' can be identified with functions in L<sup>2</sup>(''K'' / ''M'') and
<math display="block"> \chi_\lambda(g)=(\pi(g)1,1).</math>

As {{harvtxt|Kostant|1969}} proved, the representations of the spherical principal series are irreducible and two representations π<sub>λ</sub> and π<sub>μ</sub> are unitarily equivalent if and only if μ = σ(λ) for some σ in the Weyl group of ''A''.

== Example: SL(2, C) ==
The group ''G'' = SL(2,'''C''') acts transitively on the [[quaternion]]ic upper half space
<math display="block">\mathfrak{H}^3=\{x+y i + t j \mid t > 0\}</math>
by [[Möbius transformation]]s. The complex matrix
<math display="block">g=\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c& d \end{pmatrix}</math>
acts as
<math display="block">g(w) = (aw+b)(cw +d)^{-1}.</math>

The stabiliser of the point '''j''' is the maximal compact subgroup ''K'' = SU(2), so that <math>\mathfrak{H}^3 = G/K.</math> It carries the ''G''-invariant [[Riemannian metric]]

<math display="block"> ds^2 =r^{-2}\left(dx^2 + dy^2 + dr^2\right)</math>

with associated volume element

<math display="block"> dV= r^{-3}\, dx\,dy\,dr</math>

and [[Laplacian operator]]

<math display="block"> \Delta = -r^2 (\partial_x^2 + \partial_y^2 + \partial_r^2) + r\partial_r.</math>

Every point in <math>\mathfrak{H}^3</math> can be written as ''k''(''e''<sup>''t''</sup>'''j''') with ''k'' in SU(2) and ''t'' determined up to a sign. The Laplacian has the following form on functions invariant under SU(2), regarded as functions of the real parameter ''t'':
<math display="block"> \Delta= - \partial_t^2 - 2 \coth t \partial_t.</math>

The integral of an SU(2)-invariant function is given by
<math display="block">\int f \, dV= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \, \sinh^2 t \, dt.</math>

Identifying the square integrable SU(2)-invariant functions with L<sup>2</sup>('''R''') by the unitary transformation ''Uf''(''t'') = ''f''(''t'') sinh ''t'', Δ is transformed into the operator

<math display="block">U^*\Delta U = -{d^2\over dt^2} + 1.</math>

By the [[Plancherel theorem]] and [[Fourier inversion formula]] for '''R''', any SU(2)-invariant function ''f'' can be expressed in terms of the spherical functions

<math display="block">\Phi_\lambda(t)={\sin \lambda t\over \lambda \sinh t},</math>

by the spherical transform

<math display="block">\tilde{f}(\lambda)=\int f \Phi_{-\lambda} \, dV</math>

and the spherical inversion formula

<math display="block">f(x)=\int \tilde{f}(\lambda)\Phi_\lambda(x) \lambda^2 \,d\lambda.</math>

Taking <math>f = f_2^* \star f_1</math> with ''f''<sub>''i''</sub> in C<sub>c</sub>(''G'' / ''K'') and <math> f^*(g) = \overline{f(g^{-1})}</math>, and evaluating at ''i'' yields the ''Plancherel formula''

<math display="block"> \int_G f_1\overline{f_2} \, dg = \int \tilde{f}_1(\lambda) \overline{\tilde{f}_2(\lambda)}\, \lambda^2 \, d\lambda.</math>

For biinvariant functions this establishes the '''Plancherel theorem for spherical functions''': the map

<math display="block">\begin{cases}
U: L^2(K\backslash G/K) \to L^2(\R, \lambda^2\,d\lambda) \\
U: f\longmapsto \tilde{f}
\end{cases}</math>

is unitary and sends the convolution operator defined by <math>f\in L^1(K\backslash G/K)</math> into the multiplication operator defined by <math>\tilde{f}</math>.

The spherical function Φ<sub>λ</sub> is an [[eigenfunction]] of the Laplacian:

<math display="block">\Delta \Phi_\lambda= (\lambda^2 + 1) \Phi_\lambda.</math>

[[Schwartz function]]s on '''R''' are the spherical transforms of functions ''f'' belonging to the Harish-Chandra Schwartz space

<math display="block">\mathcal{S} = \left \{f \left | \sup_t \left |(1+t^2)^N(I+\Delta)^M f(t)\sinh(t) \right |<\infty \right \} \right. .</math>

By the [[Paley-Wiener theorem]], the spherical transforms of smooth SU(2)-invariant functions of [[compact support]] are precisely
functions on '''R''' which are restrictions of [[holomorphic function]]s on '''C''' satisfying an exponential growth condition

<math display="block">|F(\lambda)|\le C e^{ R \left|\operatorname{Im} \lambda\right|}.</math>

As a function on ''G'', Φ<sub>λ</sub> is the matrix coefficient of the spherical principal series defined on L<sup>2</sup>('''C'''), where '''C''' is identified with the boundary of <math>\mathfrak{H}^3</math>. The representation is given by the formula

<math display="block">\pi_\lambda(g^{-1})\xi(z)=|cz + d|^{-2-i\lambda} \xi(g(z)).</math>

The function

<math display="block">\xi_0(z)=\pi^{-1} \left (1+|z|^2 \right )^{-2}</math>

is fixed by SU(2) and

<math display="block">\Phi_\lambda(g)=(\pi_\lambda(g)\xi_0,\xi_0).</math>

The representations π<sub>λ</sub> are irreducible and unitarily equivalent only when the sign of λ is changed. The map ''W'' of <math> L^2(\mathfrak{H}^3)</math> onto {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>([0,∞) × '''C''')}} (with measure λ<sup>2</sup> ''d''λ on the first factor) given by

<math display="block"> Wf(\lambda,z)= \int_{G/K} f(g) \pi_\lambda(g)\xi_0(z) \, dg</math>

is unitary and gives the decomposition of <math> L^2({\mathfrak H}^3)</math> as a [[direct integral]] of the spherical principal series.

== Example: SL(2, R) ==
The group ''G'' = SL(2,'''R''') acts transitively on the Poincaré upper half plane

<math display="block">\mathfrak{H}^2 = \{x+r i \mid r>0\}</math>

by [[Möbius transformation]]s. The real matrix

<math display="block">g=\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c& d \end{pmatrix}</math>

acts as

<math display="block">g(w)=(aw+b)(cw +d)^{-1}.</math>

The stabiliser of the point '''i''' is the maximal compact subgroup ''K'' = SO(2), so that <math>\mathfrak{H}^2</math> = ''G'' / ''K''.
It carries the ''G''-invariant [[Riemannian metric]]

<math display="block"> ds^2 =r^{-2} \left(dx^2 + dr^2\right)</math>

with associated area element

<math display="block"> dA= r^{-2}\, dx\,dr</math>

and [[Laplacian operator]]

<math display="block"> \Delta = -r^2(\partial_x^2 + \partial_r^2).</math>

Every point in <math>\mathfrak{H}^2</math> can be written as ''k''( ''e''<sup>''t''</sup> '''i''' ) with ''k'' in SO(2) and ''t'' determined up to a sign. The Laplacian has the following form on functions invariant under SO(2), regarded as functions of the real parameter ''t'':
<math display="block"> \Delta= - \partial_t^2 - \coth t \partial_t.</math>

The integral of an SO(2)-invariant function is given by
<math display="block">\int f \, dA= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \left|\sinh t\right| dt.</math>

There are several methods for deriving the corresponding eigenfunction expansion for this ordinary differential equation including:

# the classical [[spectral theory of ordinary differential equations]] applied to the [[Spectral theory of ordinary differential equations#Application to the hypergeometric equation|hypergeometric equation]] (Mehler, Weyl, Fock);
# variants of Hadamard's method of descent, realising 2-dimensional hyperbolic space as the quotient of 3-dimensional hyperbolic space by the free action of a 1-parameter subgroup of SL(2,'''C''');
# Abel's integral equation, following Selberg and Godement;
# orbital integrals (Harish-Chandra, Gelfand & Naimark).

The second and third technique will be described below, with two different methods of descent: the classical one due Hadamard, familiar from treatments of the heat equation<ref>{{harvnb|Davies|1989}}</ref> and the wave equation<ref>{{harvnb|Lax|Phillips|1976}}</ref> on hyperbolic space; and Flensted-Jensen's method on the hyperboloid.

===Hadamard's method of descent===

If ''f''(''x'',''r'') is a function on <math>\mathfrak{H}^2</math> and

<math display="block">M_1f(x,y,r)=r^{1/2}\cdot f(x,r)</math>

then

<math display="block"> \Delta_3 M_1 f= M_1 \left (\Delta_2 + \tfrac{3}{4} \right )f,</math>

where Δ<sub>''n''</sub> is the Laplacian on <math>{\mathfrak H}^n</math>.

Since the action of SL(2,'''C''') commutes with Δ<sub>3</sub>, the operator ''M''<sub>0</sub> on S0(2)-invariant functions obtained by averaging ''M''<sub>1</sub>''f'' by the action of SU(2) also satisfies

<math display="block"> \Delta_3 M_0= M_0 \left (\Delta_2 + \tfrac{3}{4} \right).</math>

The adjoint operator ''M''<sub>1</sub>* defined by

<math display="block"> M_1^* F(x,r)=r^{1/2} \int_{-\infty}^\infty F(x,y,r)\, dy</math>

satisfies

<math display="block"> \int_{\mathfrak{H}^3} (M_1f)\cdot F \,dV = \int_{\mathfrak{H}^2} f\cdot (M_1^*F) \,dA.</math>

The adjoint ''M''<sub>0</sub>*, defined by averaging ''M''*''f'' over SO(2), satisfies
<math display="block"> \int_{\mathfrak{H}^3} (M_0f)\cdot F \,dV = \int_{\mathfrak{H}^2} f\cdot (M_0^*F) \,dA</math>
for SU(2)-invariant functions ''F'' and SO(2)-invariant functions ''f''. It follows that
<math display="block"> M_i^* \Delta_3= \left (\Delta_2 + \tfrac{3}{4} \right )M_i^*.</math>

The function
<math display="block">f_\lambda= M_1^* \Phi_\lambda</math>
is SO(2)-invariant and satisfies
<math display="block">\Delta_2 f_\lambda= \left (\lambda^2 + \tfrac{1}{4} \right )f_\lambda.</math>

On the other hand,
<math display="block">b(\lambda)=f_\lambda(i)=\int {\sin \lambda t \over \lambda \sinh t} \, dt= {\pi\over \lambda} \tanh{\pi\lambda\over 2},</math>

since the integral can be computed by integrating <math> e^{i\lambda t} /\sinh t</math> around the rectangular indented contour with vertices at ±''R'' and ±''R'' + ''πi''. Thus the eigenfunction

<math display="block">\phi_\lambda=b(\lambda)^{-1} M_1\Phi_\lambda</math>

satisfies the normalisation condition φ<sub>λ</sub>(''i'') = 1. There can only be one such solution either because the [[Wronskian]] of the ordinary differential equation must vanish or by expanding as a [[power series]] in sinh ''r''.<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=38}}</ref> It follows that

<math display="block"> \varphi_\lambda(e^t i) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \left(\cosh t - \sinh t \cos \theta\right)^{-1-i\lambda} \, d\theta.</math>

Similarly it follows that

<math display="block">\Phi_\lambda = M_1 \phi_\lambda.</math>

If the spherical transform of an SO(2)-invariant function on <math>\mathfrak{H}^2</math> is defined by

<math display="block">\tilde{f}(\lambda)=\int f \varphi_{-\lambda} \,dA,</math>

then

<math display="block"> {(M_1^* F)}^\sim(\lambda) = \tilde{F}(\lambda).</math>

Taking ''f''=''M''<sub>1</sub>*''F'', the SL(2, '''C''') inversion formula for ''F'' immediately yields

<math display="block">f(x)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty \varphi_\lambda(x) \tilde{f}(\lambda) {\lambda \pi\over 2} \tanh \left ({\pi\lambda\over 2} \right ) \, d\lambda,</math>

the spherical inversion formula for SO(2)-invariant functions on <math>\mathfrak{H}^2</math>.

As for SL(2,'''C'''), this immediately implies the Plancherel formula for ''f''<sub>i</sub> in C<sub>c</sub>(SL(2,'''R''') / SO(2)):

<math display="block">\int_{\mathfrak{H}^2} f_1\overline{f_2} \,dA = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \tilde{f}_1 \overline{\tilde{f_2}} {\lambda \pi\over 2} \tanh \left ({\pi\lambda\over 2} \right )\, d\lambda.</math>

The spherical function φ<sub>λ</sub> is an [[eigenfunction]] of the Laplacian:

<math display="block">\Delta_2 \varphi_\lambda= \left (\lambda^2 + \tfrac{1}{4} \right ) \varphi_\lambda.</math>

[[Schwartz function]]s on '''R''' are the spherical transforms of functions ''f'' belonging to the Harish-Chandra Schwartz space

<math display="block"> {\mathcal S} = \left \{f \left | \sup_t \left |(1+t^2)^N(I+\Delta)^M f(t)\varphi_0(t) \right |<\infty \right \} \right. .</math>

The spherical transforms of smooth SO(2)-invariant functions of [[compact support]] are precisely functions on '''R''' which are restrictions of [[holomorphic function]]s on '''C''' satisfying an exponential growth condition

<math display="block">|F(\lambda)|\le C e^{R|\Im\lambda|}.</math>

Both these results can be deduced by descent from the corresponding results for SL(2,'''C'''),<ref name="FlenstedJensen1978">{{harvnb|Flensted-Jensen|1978}}</ref> by verifying directly that the spherical transform satisfies the given growth conditions<ref>{{harvnb|Anker|1991}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Jorgenson|Lang|2001}}</ref> and then using the relation <math>(M_1^* F)^\sim = \tilde{F}</math>.

As a function on ''G'', φ<sub>λ</sub> is the matrix coefficient of the spherical principal series defined on L<sup>2</sup>('''R'''), where '''R''' is identified with the boundary of <math>\mathfrak{H}^2</math>. The representation is given by the formula

<math display="block">\pi_\lambda(g^{-1})\xi(x)=|cx + d|^{-1-i\lambda} \xi(g(x)).</math>

The function

<math display="block">\xi_0(x) = \pi^{-1} \left(1+|x|^2\right)^{-1}</math>

is fixed by SO(2) and

<math display="block">\Phi_\lambda(g)=(\pi_\lambda(g)\xi_0,\xi_0).</math>

The representations π<sub>λ</sub> are irreducible and unitarily equivalent only when the sign of λ is changed. The map <math>W: L^2({\mathfrak H}^2) \to L^2 ([0,\infty) \times \R)</math> with measure <math display="inline">\frac{\lambda\pi}{2} \tanh \left( \frac{\pi\lambda}{2} \right )\, d\lambda</math> on the first factor, is given by the formula

<math display="block"> Wf(\lambda,x)= \int_{G/K} f(g) \pi_\lambda(g)\xi_0(x) \, dg</math>

is unitary and gives the decomposition of <math>L^2(\mathfrak{H}^2)</math> as a [[direct integral]] of the spherical principal series.

===Flensted–Jensen's method of descent===

Hadamard's method of descent relied on functions invariant under the action of 1-parameter subgroup of translations in the ''y'' parameter in <math>\mathfrak{H}^3</math>. Flensted&ndash;Jensen's method uses the centraliser of SO(2) in SL(2,'''C''') which splits as a direct product of SO(2) and the 1-parameter subgroup ''K''<sub>1</sub> of matrices

<math display="block">g_t=\begin{pmatrix} \cosh t & i\sinh t \\ -i\sinh t& \cosh t\end{pmatrix}.</math>

The symmetric space SL(2,'''C''')/SU(2) can be identified with the space '''H'''<sup>3</sup> of positive 2×2 matrices ''A'' with determinant 1
<math display="block">A=\begin{pmatrix} a+b & x+iy \\ x-iy & a -b\end{pmatrix}</math>
with the group action given by
<math display="block">g\cdot A = gAg^*. </math>

Thus
<math display="block"> g_t\cdot A=\begin{pmatrix} a \cosh 2t +y \sinh 2t +b & x+i(y\cosh 2t + a\sinh 2t) \\ x-i(y\cosh 2t + a\sinh 2t) & a\cosh 2t +y \sinh 2t -b\end{pmatrix}.</math>

So on the [[hyperboloid]] <math>a^2=1+b^2 +x^2 +y^2 </math>, ''g''<sub>''t''</sub> only changes the coordinates ''y'' and ''a''. Similarly the action of SO(2) acts by rotation on the coordinates (''b'',''x'') leaving ''a'' and ''y'' unchanged. The space '''H'''<sup>2</sup> of real-valued positive matrices ''A'' with ''y'' = 0 can be identified with the orbit of the identity matrix under SL(2,'''R'''). Taking coordinates (''b'',''x'',''y'') in '''H'''<sup>3</sup> and (''b'',''x'') on '''H'''<sup>2</sup> the volume and area elements are given by

<math display="block">dV =(1+r^2)^{-1/2} \,db\, dx\, dy,\,\,\, dA= (1+r^2)^{-1/2} \,db\, dx,</math>

where ''r''<sup>2</sup> equals ''b''<sup>2</sup> + ''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup> or ''b''<sup>2</sup> + ''x''<sup>2</sup>,
so that ''r'' is related to hyperbolic distance from the origin by <math> r =\sinh t</math>.

The [[Laplacian operator]]s are given by the formula

<math display="block">\Delta_n=-L_n - R_n^2 -(n-1)R_n, \, </math>

where

<math display="block">L_2=\partial_b^2 +\partial_x^2, \,\,\, R_2=b\partial_b + x\partial_x</math>

and

<math display="block">L_3=\partial_b^2 +\partial_x^2 +\partial_y^2,\,\, \, R_3=b\partial_b + x\partial_x + y\partial_y. \, </math>

For an SU(2)-invariant function ''F'' on '''H'''<sup>3</sup> and an SO(2)-invariant function on '''H'''<sup>2</sup>, regarded as functions of ''r'' or ''t'',

<math display="block">\int_{H^3} F \,dV =4\pi \int_{-\infty}^\infty F(t) \sinh^2 t \, dt,\,\,\, \int_{H^2} f \,dV =2\pi\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t) \sinh t \, dt.</math>

If ''f''(''b'',''x'') is a function on '''H'''<sup>2</sup>, ''Ef'' is defined by

<math display="block">Ef(b,x,y)=f(b,x). \, </math>

Thus

<math display="block">\Delta_3 Ef = E(\Delta_2 - R_2)f. \, </math>

If ''f'' is SO(2)-invariant, then, regarding ''f'' as a function of ''r'' or ''t'',

<math display="block"> (-\Delta_2 +R_2)f= \partial_t^2 f + \coth t \partial _t f + r\partial_r f =\partial_t^2 f + (\coth t + \tanh t)\partial_t f.</math>

On the other hand,
<math display="block">\partial_t^2 + (\coth t + \tanh t)\partial_t =\partial_t^2 + 2 \coth(2t) \partial_t.</math>

Thus, setting ''Sf''(''t'') = ''f''(2''t''),
<math display="block">(\Delta_2 -R_2)Sf = 4S\Delta_2f,</math>
leading to the fundamental ''descent relation'' of Flensted-Jensen for ''M''<sub>0</sub> = ''ES'':
<math display="block">\Delta_3 M_0 f = 4M_0\Delta_2 f.</math>

The same relation holds with ''M''<sub>0</sub> by ''M'', where ''Mf'' is obtained by averaging ''M''<sub>0</sub>''f'' over SU(2).

The extension ''Ef'' is constant in the ''y'' variable and therefore invariant under the transformations ''g''<sub>''s''</sub>. On the other hand, for ''F'' a suitable function on '''H'''<sup>3</sup>, the function ''QF'' defined by
<math display="block"> QF = \int_{K_1}F\circ g_s \, ds</math>
is independent of the ''y'' variable. A straightforward change of variables shows that
<math display="block"> \int_{H^3}F \, dV = \int_{H^2} (1+b^2 +x^2)^{1/2} QF \, dA.</math>

Since ''K''<sub>1</sub> commutes with SO(2), ''QF'' is SO(2)--invariant if ''F'' is, in particular if ''F'' is SU(2)-invariant. In this case ''QF'' is a function of ''r'' or ''t'', so that ''M''*''F'' can be defined by
<math display="block"> M^*F(t)=QF(t/2).</math>

The integral formula above then yields
<math display="block">\int_{H^3} F \, dV = \int_{H^2} M^*F \, dA</math>
and hence, since for ''f'' SO(2)-invariant,
<math display="block">M^*((Mf)\cdot F) =f \cdot (M^*F),</math>
the following adjoint formula:
<math display="block">\int_{H^3} (Mf)\cdot F \, dV =\int_{H^2} f\cdot (M*F)\, dV.</math>

As a consequence
<math display="block">M^*\Delta_3 = 4\Delta_2M^*.</math>

Thus, as in the case of Hadamard's method of descent.

<math display="block">M^*\Phi_{2\lambda} =b(\lambda) \varphi_\lambda</math>
with
<math display="block">b(\lambda)=M^*\Phi_{2\lambda}(0)=\pi \tanh \pi \lambda</math>
and
<math display="block">\Phi_{2\lambda}=M\varphi_\lambda.</math>

It follows that
<math display="block"> {(M^* F)}^\sim(\lambda) = \tilde{F}(2\lambda).</math>

Taking ''f''=''M''*''F'', the SL(2,'''C''') inversion formula for ''F'' then immediately yields
<math display="block">f(x)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty \varphi_\lambda(x) \tilde{f}(\lambda)\,{\lambda \pi\over 2} \tanh\left(\frac{\pi\lambda}{2}\right)\, d\lambda,</math>

===Abel's integral equation===

The spherical function φ<sub>λ</sub> is given by
<math display="block">\varphi_\lambda(g)=\int_K \alpha'(kg) \, dk,</math>
so that
<math display="block"> \tilde{f}(\lambda)=\int_S f(s) \alpha'(s)\, ds,</math>

Thus
<math display="block">\tilde{f}(\lambda)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_0^\infty f\!\left(\frac{a^2 + a^{-2} +b^2}{2}\right)a^{-i\lambda/2} \, da\,db,</math>

so that defining ''F'' by

<math display="block">F(u)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f\!\left(u + \frac{t^2}{2}\right) \, dt,</math>

the spherical transform can be written

<math display="block">\tilde{f}(\lambda)=\int_0^\infty F\!\left(\frac{a^2+a^{-2}}{2}\right) a^{-i\lambda}\, da= \int_0^\infty F(\cosh t)e^{-it\lambda} \, dt.</math>

The relation between ''F'' and ''f'' is classically inverted by the [[Abel integral equation]]:

<math display="block">f(x)= \frac{-1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^\infty F'\!\left(x +{t^2\over 2}\right)\, dt.</math>

In fact<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=41}}</ref>

<math display="block">\int_{-\infty}^\infty F'\!\left(x + \frac{t^2}{2}\right)\, dt
= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty f'\!\left(x + \frac{t^2 + u^2}{2}\right) \, dt\,du
={2\pi} \int_0^\infty f'\!\left(x + \frac{r^2}{2}\right) r\, dr
= -2\pi f(x).</math>

The relation between ''F'' and <math>\tilde{f}</math> is inverted by the [[Fourier inversion formula]]:

<math display="block">F(\cosh t)={2\over \pi} \int_0^\infty\tilde{f}(i\lambda)\cos(\lambda t) \, d\lambda.</math>

Hence

<math display="block">f(i)={1\over 2\pi^2} \int_0^\infty \tilde{f}(\lambda) \lambda\, d\lambda \int_{-\infty}^\infty {\sin \lambda t/2\over \sinh t} \cosh {t\over 2} \, dt ={1\over 2\pi^2} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \tilde{f}(\lambda) {\lambda\pi\over 2} \tanh\left({\pi\lambda\over 2}\right)\, d\lambda.</math>

This gives the spherical inversion for the point ''i''. Now for fixed ''g'' in SL(2,'''R''') define<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=46}}</ref>

<math display="block">f_1(w)=\int_K f(gkw) \, dk,</math>

another rotation invariant function on <math>\mathfrak{H}^2</math> with ''f''<sub>1</sub>(i)=''f''(''g''(''i'')). On the other hand, for biinvariant functions ''f'',

<math display="block">\pi_\lambda(f)\xi_0 =\tilde{f}(\lambda) \xi_0</math>

so that

<math display="block"> \tilde{f}_1(\lambda)=\tilde{f}(\lambda)\cdot \varphi_\lambda(w),</math>

where ''w'' = ''g''(''i''). Combining this with the above inversion formula for ''f''<sub>1</sub> yields the general spherical inversion formula:

<math display="block"> f(w) ={1\over \pi^2} \int_0^\infty \tilde{f}(\lambda) \varphi_\lambda(w) {\lambda\pi\over 2} \tanh\left({\pi\lambda\over 2}\right)\, d\lambda.</math>

==Other special cases==
All complex semisimple Lie groups or the [[Lorentz group]]s SO<sup>0</sup>(''N'',1) with ''N'' odd can be treated directly by reduction to the usual Fourier transform.<ref name="FlenstedJensen1978" /><ref>{{harvnb|Takahashi|1963}}</ref> The remaining real Lorentz groups can be deduced by Flensted-Jensen's method of descent, as can other semisimple Lie groups of real rank one.<ref>{{harvnb|Loeb|1979}}</ref> Flensted-Jensen's method of descent also applies to the treatment of real semisimple Lie groups for which the Lie algebras are [[real form (Lie theory)#Normal real form|normal real forms]] of complex semisimple Lie algebras.<ref name="FlenstedJensen1978" /> The special case of SL(N,'''R''') is treated in detail in {{harvtxt|Jorgenson|Lang|2001}}; this group is also the normal real form of SL(N,'''C''').

The approach of {{harvtxt|Flensted-Jensen|1978}} applies to a wide class of real semisimple Lie groups of arbitrary real rank and yields the explicit product form of the Plancherel measure on <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>* without using Harish-Chandra's expansion of the spherical functions φ<sub>λ</sub>
in terms of his c-function, discussed below. Although less general, it gives a simpler approach to the Plancherel theorem for this class of groups.

===Complex semisimple Lie groups===

If ''G'' is a complex semisimple Lie group, it is the [[complexification]] of its maximal compact subgroup ''U'', a compact semisimple Lie group. If <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{u}</math> are their Lie algebras, then <math> \mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{u} \oplus i\mathfrak{u}.</math> Let ''T'' be a [[maximal torus]] in ''U'' with Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{t}.</math> Then setting

<math display="block">A= \exp i \mathfrak{t}, \qquad P= \exp i \mathfrak{u},</math>

there is the [[Cartan decomposition]]:

<math display="block">G=P\cdot U = UAU.</math>

The finite-dimensional irreducible representations π<sub>λ</sub> of ''U'' are indexed by certain λ in <math>\mathfrak{t}^*</math>.<ref>These are indexed by highest weights shifted by half the sum of the positive roots.</ref> The corresponding character formula and dimension formula of [[Hermann Weyl]] give explicit formulas for

<math display="block">\chi_\lambda(e^X) = \operatorname{Tr} \pi_\lambda(e^X), (X\in \mathfrak{t}), \qquad d(\lambda)=\dim \pi_\lambda.</math>

These formulas, initially defined on <math>\mathfrak{t}^*\times \mathfrak{t}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{t}^*</math>, extend holomorphic to their  complexifications. Moreover,

<math display="block">\chi_\lambda(e^X)={\sum_{\sigma \in W} {\rm sign}(\sigma) e^{i\lambda(\sigma X)}\over \delta(e^X)},</math>

where ''W'' is the [[Weyl group]] <math> W =N_U(T)/T</math> and δ(''e''<sup>''X''</sup>) is given by a product formula (Weyl's denominator formula) which extends holomorphically to the complexification of <math>\mathfrak{t}</math>. There is a similar product formula for ''d''(λ), a polynomial in λ.

On the complex group ''G'', the integral of a ''U''-biinvariant function ''F'' can be evaluated as

<math display="block">\int_G F(g) \, dg = {1\over |W|} \int_{\mathfrak{a}} F(e^X)\, |\delta(e^X)|^2 \, dX.</math>

where <math>\mathfrak{a}=i\mathfrak{t}</math>.

The spherical functions of ''G'' are labelled by λ in <math>\mathfrak{a}=i\mathfrak{t}^*</math> and given by the Harish-Chandra-Berezin formula<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|pages=423–433}}</ref>

<math display="block"> \Phi_\lambda(e^X) = {\chi_\lambda(e^X)\over d(\lambda)}.</math>

They are the matrix coefficients of the irreducible spherical principal series of ''G'' induced from the character of the [[Borel subgroup]] of ''G'' corresponding to λ; these representations are irreducible and can all be realized on L<sup>2</sup>(''U''/''T'').

The spherical transform of a ''U''-biinvariant function ''F'' is given by

<math display="block"> \tilde{F}(\lambda)=\int_G F(g) \Phi_{-\lambda}(g)\, dg</math>

and the spherical inversion formula by

<math display="block"> F(g) ={1\over |W|}\int_{{\mathfrak a}^*} \tilde{F}(\lambda)\Phi_\lambda(g) |d(\lambda)|^2 \, d\,\lambda=
\int_{{\mathfrak a}^*_+} \tilde{F}(\lambda)\Phi_\lambda(g) |d(\lambda)|^2 \, d\,\lambda,</math>

where <math>{\mathfrak a}^*_+</math> is a [[Weyl chamber]]. In fact the result follows from the [[Fourier inversion formula]] on <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> since<ref>{{harvnb|Flensted-Jensen|1978|page=115}}</ref>
<math display="block">d(\lambda)\delta(e^X)\Phi_\lambda(e^X)=\sum_{\sigma\in W} {\rm sign}(\sigma) e^{i\lambda(X)},</math>
so that <math>\overline{d(\lambda)}\tilde{F}(\lambda)</math> is just the [[Fourier transform]] of <math> F(e^X)\delta(e^X)</math>.

Note that the [[symmetric space]] ''G''/''U'' has as ''compact dual''<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1978}}</ref> the compact symmetric space ''U'' x ''U'' / ''U'', where ''U'' is the diagonal subgroup. The spherical functions for the latter space, which can be identified with ''U'' itself, are the normalized characters χ<sub>λ</sub>/''d''(λ) indexed by lattice points in the interior of <math>\mathfrak {a}^*_+</math> and the role of ''A'' is played by ''T''. The spherical transform of ''f'' of a [[class function]] on ''U'' is given by

<math display="block"> \tilde{f}(\lambda)=\int_U f(u){\overline{\chi_\lambda(u)}\over d(\lambda)} \,du</math>

and the spherical inversion formula now follows from the theory of [[Fourier series]] on ''T'':

<math display="block"> f(u)=\sum_{\lambda} \tilde{f}(\lambda) {\chi_\lambda(u)\over d(\lambda)} d(\lambda)^2.</math>

There is an evident duality between these formulas and those for the non-compact dual.<ref>The spherical inversion formula for ''U'' is equivalent to the statement that the functions <math>\chi_\lambda d(\lambda)^{-1/2}</math> form an [[orthonormal basis]] for the class functions.</ref>

===Real semisimple Lie groups===

Let ''G''<sub>0</sub> be a [[Real form (Lie theory)#Normal real form|normal real form]] of the complex semisimple Lie group ''G'', the fixed points of an involution σ, conjugate linear on the Lie algebra of ''G''. Let τ be a Cartan involution of ''G''<sub>0</sub> extended to an involution of ''G'', complex linear on its Lie algebra, chosen to commute with σ. The fixed point subgroup of τσ is a compact real form ''U'' of ''G'', intersecting ''G''<sub>0</sub> in a maximal compact subgroup ''K''<sub>0</sub>. The fixed point subgroup of τ is ''K'', the complexification of ''K''<sub>0</sub>. Let ''G''<sub>0</sub>= ''K''<sub>0</sub>·''P''<sub>0</sub> be the corresponding Cartan decomposition of ''G''<sub>0</sub> and let ''A'' be a maximal Abelian subgroup of ''P''<sub>0</sub>. {{harvtxt|Flensted-Jensen|1978}} proved that
<math display="block"> G = K A_+ U,</math>
where ''A''<sub>+</sub> is the image of the closure of a Weyl chamber in <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> under the exponential map. Moreover,
<math display="block"> K\backslash G/U = A_+.</math>

Since
<math display="block"> K_0\backslash G_0/K_0 = A_+</math>

it follows that there is a canonical identification between ''K'' \ ''G'' / ''U'', ''K''<sub>0</sub> \ ''G''<sub>0</sub> /''K''<sub>0</sub> and ''A''<sub>+</sub>. Thus ''K''<sub>0</sub>-biinvariant functions on ''G''<sub>0</sub> can be identified with functions on ''A''<sub>+</sub> as can functions on ''G'' that are left invariant under ''K'' and right invariant under ''U''. Let ''f'' be a function in <math>C^\infty_c(K_0\backslash G_0 /K_0)</math> and define ''Mf'' in <math>C^\infty_c(U\backslash G /U)</math> by
<math display="block"> Mf(a)=\int_U f(ua^2) \,du.</math>

Here a third Cartan decomposition of ''G'' = ''UAU'' has been used to identify ''U'' \ ''G'' / ''U'' with ''A''<sub>+</sub>.

Let Δ be the Laplacian on ''G''<sub>0</sub>/''K''<sub>0</sub> and let Δ<sub>c</sub> be the Laplacian on ''G''/''U''. Then
<math display="block"> 4M\Delta = \Delta_c M.</math>

For ''F'' in <math>C^\infty_c(U\backslash G /U)</math>, define ''M''*''F'' in <math>C^\infty_c(K_0\backslash G_0 /K_0)</math> by
<math display="block"> M^*F(a^2)=\int_K F(ga) \, dg.</math>

Then ''M'' and ''M''* satisfy the duality relations
<math display="block"> \int_{G/U} (Mf) \cdot F = \int_{G_0/K_0} f\cdot (M^*F).</math>

In particular
<math display="block"> M^*\Delta_c= 4\Delta M^*.</math>

There is a similar compatibility for other operators in the center of the [[universal enveloping algebra]] of ''G''<sub>0</sub>. It follows from the eigenfunction characterisation of spherical functions that <math> M^*\Phi_{2\lambda}</math> is proportional to φ<sub>λ</sub> on ''G''<sub>0</sub>, the constant of proportionality being given by
<math display="block"> b(\lambda)=M^*\Phi_{2\lambda}(1)=\int_K \Phi_{2\lambda}(k)\, dk. </math>

Moreover, in this case<ref>{{harvnb|Flensted-Jensen|1978|page=133}}</ref>
<math display="block"> (M^* F)^\sim(\lambda)= \tilde{F}(2\lambda).</math>

If ''f'' = ''M''*''F'', then the spherical inversion formula for ''F'' on ''G'' implies that for ''f'' on ''G''<sub>0</sub>:<ref>{{harvnb|Flensted-Jensen|1978|page=133}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=490–491}}</ref>
<math display="block"> f(g)= \int_{\mathfrak{a}^*_+} \tilde{f}(\lambda) \varphi_\lambda(g) \,\, 2^{{\rm dim}\, A}\cdot |b(\lambda)|\cdot |d(2\lambda)|^2 \,d\lambda, </math>
since
<math display="block">f(g)= M^*F(g)= \int_{\mathfrak{a}_+^*} \tilde{F}(2\lambda) M^*\Phi_{2\lambda}(g) 2^{{\rm dim}\, A} |d(2\lambda)|^2 \, d\lambda
= \int_{\mathfrak{a}_+^*} \tilde{f}(\lambda) \varphi_\lambda(g) \,\,b(\lambda) 2^{{\rm dim}\, A} |d(2\lambda)|^2 \, d\lambda.
</math>

The direct calculation of the integral for ''b''(λ), generalising the computation of {{harvtxt|Godement|1957}} for SL(2,'''R'''), was left as an open problem by {{harvtxt|Flensted-Jensen|1978}}.<ref>''b''(λ) can be written as integral over ''A''<sub>0</sub> where ''K'' = ''K''<sub>0</sub> ''A''<sub>0</sub> ''K''<sub>0</sub> is the Cartan decomposition of ''K''. The integral then becomes an alternating sum of multidimensional Godement-type integrals, whose combinatorics is governed by that of the [[Zonal spherical function#Cartan–Helgason theorem|Cartan-Helgason theorem]] for ''U''/''K''<sub>0</sub>. An equivalent computation that arises in the theory of the [[Radon transform]] has been discussed by {{harvtxt|Beerends|1987}}, {{harvtxt|Stade|1999}} and {{harvtxt|Gindikin|2008}}.</ref> An explicit product formula for ''b''(λ) was known from the prior determination of the Plancherel measure by {{harvtxt|Harish-Chandra|1966}}, giving<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Beerends|1987|page=4–5}}</ref>
<math display="block"> b(\lambda) =C\cdot d(2\lambda)^{-1}\cdot \prod_{\alpha>0} \tanh {\pi(\alpha,\lambda)\over (\alpha,\alpha)},</math>

where α ranges over the positive roots of the [[root system]] in <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> and ''C'' is a normalising constant, given as a quotient of products of [[Gamma function]]s.

==Harish-Chandra's Plancherel theorem==
Let ''G'' be a noncompact connected real semisimple Lie group with finite center. Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> denote its Lie algebra. Let ''K'' be a maximal compact subgroup
given as the subgroup of fixed points of a Cartan involution σ. Let <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\pm}</math> be the ±1 eigenspaces of σ in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, so that <math>\mathfrak{k}=\mathfrak{g}_+</math> is the Lie algebra of ''K'' and <math>\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{g}_-</math> give the Cartan decomposition

<math display="block">\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{k}+\mathfrak{p},\,\, G=\exp \mathfrak{p}\cdot K.</math>

Let <math>\mathfrak {a}</math> be a maximal Abelian subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> and for α in <math>\mathfrak {a}^*</math> let

<math display="block">\mathfrak{g}_\alpha=\{X\in \mathfrak{g}: [H,X]=\alpha(H)X\,\,(H\in \mathfrak{a})\}.</math>

If α ≠ 0 and <math>\mathfrak{g}_\alpha\ne (0)</math>, then α is called a ''restricted root'' and <math>m_\alpha = \dim \mathfrak{g}_\alpha</math> is called its ''multiplicity''. Let ''A'' = exp <math>\mathfrak {a}</math>, so that ''G'' = ''KAK''.The restriction of the [[Killing form]] defines an inner product on <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> and hence <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>, which allows <math>\mathfrak{a}^*</math> to be identified with <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>. With respect to this inner product, the restricted roots Σ give a [[root system]]. Its [[Weyl group]] can be identified with <math>W = N_K(A) / C_K(A)</math>. A choice of positive roots defines a Weyl chamber <math>\mathfrak{a}_+^*</math>. The ''reduced root system'' Σ<sub>0</sub> consists of roots α such that α/2 is not a root.

Defining the spherical functions φ<sub> λ</sub> as above for λ in <math>\mathfrak {a}^*</math>, the spherical transform of ''f'' in C<sub>c</sub><sup>∞</sup>(''K'' \ ''G'' / ''K'') is defined by
<math display="block">\tilde{f}(\lambda)=\int_G f(g) \varphi_{-\lambda}(g)\, dg.</math>

The '''spherical inversion formula''' states that
<math display="block">f(g)=\int_{\mathfrak{a}^*_+} \tilde{f}(\lambda) \varphi_\lambda(g)\, |c(\lambda)|^{-2}\, d\lambda,</math>
where '''Harish-Chandra's c-function''' '''c'''(λ) is defined by<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=447}}</ref>
<math display="block">c(\lambda)=c_0\cdot\prod_{\alpha\in \Sigma_0^+} \frac{2^{-i(\lambda,\alpha_0)}
\Gamma(i(\lambda,\alpha_0))}{
\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{2} m_\alpha + 1 +i(\lambda,\alpha_0)\right]\right)
\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{2} m_{\alpha} + m_{2\alpha} +i(\lambda,\alpha_0)\right]\right)}</math>
with <math>\alpha_0=(\alpha,\alpha)^{-1} \alpha</math> and the constant ''c''<sub>0</sub> chosen so that '''c'''(−''iρ'') = 1 where
<math display="block"> \rho = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\alpha\in \Sigma^+} m_\alpha \alpha.</math>

The '''Plancherel theorem for spherical functions''' states that the map
<math display="block">W:f\mapsto \tilde{f},\,\,\,\ L^2(K\backslash G /K) \rightarrow L^2(\mathfrak{a}_+^*, |c(\lambda)|^{-2}\, d\lambda)</math>
is unitary and transforms convolution by <math> f\in L^1(K\backslash G/K)</math> into multiplication by <math>\tilde{f}</math>.

==Harish-Chandra's spherical function expansion==
Since ''G'' = ''KAK'', functions on ''G''/''K'' that are invariant under ''K'' can be identified with functions on ''A'', and hence <math>\mathfrak a</math>, that are invariant under the Weyl group ''W''. In particular since the Laplacian Δ on ''G''/''K'' commutes with the action of ''G'', it defines a second order differential operator ''L'' on <math>\mathfrak a</math>, invariant under ''W'', called the ''radial part of the Laplacian''. In general if ''X'' is in <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>, it defines a first order differential operator (or vector field) by
<math display="block">Xf(y)=\left.\frac{d}{dt} f(y + tX)\right|_{t=0}.</math>

''L'' can be expressed in terms of these operators by the formula<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=267}}</ref>
<math display="block">L = \Delta_{\mathfrak{a}} - \sum_{\alpha>0} m_\alpha \, \coth \alpha \, A_\alpha,</math>
where ''A''<sub>α</sub> in <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> is defined by
<math display="block"> (A_\alpha,X)=\alpha(X)</math>
and
<math display="block">\Delta_{\mathfrak{a}} = -\sum X_i^2</math>
is the Laplacian on <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>, corresponding to any choice of orthonormal basis (''X''<sub>''i''</sub>).

Thus
<math display="block">L=L_0 -\sum_{\alpha>0} m_\alpha\, (\coth \alpha -1) A_\alpha,</math>
where
<math display="block">L_0=\Delta_{\mathfrak{a}} - \sum_{\alpha>0} A_\alpha,</math>
so that ''L'' can be regarded as a perturbation of the constant-coefficient operator ''L''<sub>0</sub>.

Now the spherical function φ<sub>λ</sub> is an eigenfunction of the Laplacian:
<math display="block">\Delta\varphi_\lambda=\left(\left\|\lambda\right\|^2 + \left\|\rho\right\|^2\right)\varphi_\lambda</math>
and therefore of ''L'', when viewed as a ''W''-invariant function on <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>.

Since ''e''<sup>''iλ''–''ρ''</sup> and its transforms under ''W'' are eigenfunctions of ''L''<sub>0</sub> with the same eigenvalue, it is natural look for a formula for φ<sub>λ</sub> in terms of a perturbation series
<math display="block">f_\lambda=e^{i\lambda -\rho}\sum_{\mu\in \Lambda} a_\mu(\lambda) e^{-\mu},</math>
with Λ the cone of all non-negative integer combinations of positive roots, and the transforms of ''f''<sub>λ</sub> under ''W''. The expansion
<math display="block">\coth x-1 =2 \sum_{m>0} e^{-2mx},</math>

leads to a recursive formula for the coefficients ''a''<sub>μ</sub>(λ). In particular they are uniquely determined and the
series and its derivatives converges absolutely on <math>\mathfrak{a}_+</math>, a [[fundamental domain]] for ''W''. Remarkably it turns out that ''f''<sub>λ</sub> is also an eigenfunction of the other ''G''-invariant differential operators on ''G''/''K'', each of which induces a ''W''-invariant differential operator on <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>.

It follows that φ<sub>λ</sub> can be expressed in terms as a linear combination of ''f''<sub>λ</sub> and its transforms under ''W'':<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=430}}</ref>
<math display="block">\varphi_\lambda=\sum_{s\in W} c(s\lambda) f_{s\lambda}.</math>

Here '''c'''(λ) is '''Harish-Chandra's c-function'''. It describes the asymptotic behaviour of φ<sub>λ</sub> in <math>\mathfrak{a}_+</math>,  since<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=435}}</ref>
<math display="block">\varphi_\lambda(e^tX) \sim c(\lambda) e^{(i\lambda -\rho)Xt}</math>
for ''X'' in <math>\mathfrak{a}_+</math> and ''t'' > 0 large.

Harish-Chandra obtained a second integral formula for φ<sub>λ</sub> and hence '''c'''(λ) using the [[Bruhat decomposition]] of ''G'':<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1978|page=403}}</ref>
<math display="block">G = \bigcup_{s\in W} B s B,</math>

where ''B'' = ''MAN'' and the union is disjoint. Taking the [[Coxeter element]] ''s''<sub>0</sub> of ''W'', the unique element mapping <math>\mathfrak{a}_+</math> onto <math>-\mathfrak{a}_+</math>, it follows that σ(''N'') has a dense open orbit ''G''/''B'' = ''K''/''M'' whose complement is a union of cells of strictly smaller dimension and therefore has measure zero. It follows that the integral formula
for φ<sub>λ</sub> initially defined over ''K''/''M''

<math display="block">\varphi_\lambda(g) = \int_{K/M} \lambda'(gk)^{-1}\, dk.</math>

can be transferred to σ(''N''):<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=436}}</ref>
<math display="block">\varphi_\lambda(e^X) = e^{i\lambda -\rho} \int_{\sigma(N)} {\overline{\lambda'(n)} \over \lambda'(e^Xne^{-X})} \, dn,</math>
for ''X'' in <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>.

Since
<math display="block">\lim_{t\to \infty} e^{tX} n e^{-tX} = 1</math>

for ''X'' in <math>\mathfrak{a}_+</math>, the asymptotic behaviour of φ<sub>λ</sub> can be read off from this integral, leading to the formula:<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=447}}</ref>
<math display="block"> c(\lambda)=\int_{\sigma(N)} \overline{\lambda'(n)}\, dn.</math>

==Harish-Chandra's c-function==

{{main article|Harish-Chandra's c-function}}

The many roles of Harish-Chandra's '''c'''-function in [[non-commutative harmonic analysis]] are surveyed in {{harvtxt|Helgason|2000}}. Although it was originally introduced by Harish-Chandra in the asymptotic expansions of spherical functions, discussed above, it was also soon understood to be intimately related to intertwining operators between induced representations, first studied in this context by {{harvtxt|Bruhat|1956}}. These operators exhibit the unitary equivalence between π<sub>λ</sub> and π<sub>''s''λ</sub> for ''s'' in the Weyl group and a '''c'''-function '''c'''<sub>''s''</sub>(λ) can be attached to each such operator: namely the value at ''1'' of the intertwining operator applied to ξ<sub>0</sub>, the constant function 1, in L<sup>2</sup>(''K''/''M'').<ref>{{harvnb|Knapp|2001}}, Chapter VII</ref> Equivalently, since ξ<sub>0</sub> is up to scalar multiplication the unique vector fixed by ''K'', it is an eigenvector of the intertwining operator with eigenvalue '''c'''<sub>''s''</sub>(λ).
These operators all act on the same space L<sup>2</sup>(''K''/''M''), which can be identified with the representation induced from the 1-dimensional representation defined by λ on ''MAN''. Once ''A'' has been chosen, the compact subgroup ''M'' is uniquely determined as the centraliser of ''A'' in ''K''. The nilpotent subgroup ''N'', however, depends on a choice of a Weyl chamber in <math>\mathfrak{a}^*</math>, the various choices being permuted by the Weyl group ''W'' = ''M'' ' / ''M'', where ''M'' ' is the normaliser of ''A'' in ''K''. The '''standard intertwining operator''' corresponding to (''s'', λ) is defined on the induced representation by<ref>{{harvnb|Knapp|2001|page=177}}</ref>
<math display="block"> A(s,\lambda)F(k)=\int_{\sigma(N)\cap s^{-1}Ns} F(ksn)\, dn,</math>
where σ is the Cartan involution. It satisfies the intertwining relation
<math display="block"> A(s,\lambda)\pi_\lambda(g) =\pi_{s\lambda}(g) A(s,\lambda).</math>

The key property of the intertwining operators and their integrals is the multiplicative cocycle property<ref>{{harvnb|Knapp|2001|page=182}}</ref>
<math display="block"> A(s_1s_2,\lambda) = A(s_1,s_2\lambda) A(s_2,\lambda),</math>
whenever
<math display="block">\ell(s_1s_2) = \ell(s_1) + \ell(s_2)</math>

for the length function on the Weyl group associated with the choice of Weyl chamber. For ''s'' in ''W'', this is the number of chambers crossed by the straight line segment between ''X'' and ''sX'' for any point ''X'' in the interior of the chamber. The unique element of greatest length ''s''<sub>0</sub>, namely the number of positive restricted roots, is the unique element that carries the Weyl chamber <math>\mathfrak{a}_+^*</math> onto <math>-\mathfrak{a}_+^*</math>. By Harish-Chandra's integral formula, it corresponds to Harish-Chandra's '''c'''-function:

<math display="block"> c(\lambda)=c_{s_0}(\lambda).</math>

The '''c'''-functions are in general defined by the equation
<math display="block"> A(s,\lambda)\xi_0 =c_s(\lambda)\xi_0,</math>
where ξ<sub>0</sub> is the constant function 1 in ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''K''/''M''). The cocycle property of the intertwining operators implies a similar multiplicative property for the '''c'''-functions:
<math display="block"> c_{s_1s_2}(\lambda) =c_{s_1}(s_2 \lambda)c_{s_2}(\lambda)</math>
provided
<math display="block">\ell(s_1 s_2) = \ell(s_1) + \ell(s_2).</math>

This reduces the computation of '''c'''<sub>''s''</sub> to the case when ''s'' = ''s''<sub>α</sub>, the reflection in a (simple) root α, the so-called "rank-one reduction" of {{harvtxt|Gindikin|Karpelevich|1962}}. In fact the integral involves only the closed connected subgroup ''G''<sup>α</sup> corresponding to the Lie subalgebra generated by <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\pm \alpha}</math> where α lies in Σ<sub>0</sub><sup>+</sup>.<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1978|page=407}}</ref> Then ''G''<sup>α</sup> is a real semisimple Lie group with real rank one, i.e. dim ''A''<sup>α</sup> = 1, and '''c'''<sub>''s''</sub> is just the Harish-Chandra '''c'''-function of ''G''<sup>α</sup>. In this case the '''c'''-function can be computed directly by various means:

*by noting that φ<sub>λ</sub> can be expressed in terms of the [[hypergeometric function]] for which the asymptotic expansion is known from the classical formulas of [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] for the [[Hypergeometric differential equation#Connection coefficients|connection coefficients]];<ref name="HarishChandra1958" /><ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=484}}</ref>
*by directly computing the integral, which can be expressed as an integral in two variables and hence a product of two [[beta function]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1978|page=414}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=437}}</ref>

This yields the following formula:
<math display="block">c_{s_\alpha}(\lambda) = c_0 \frac{2^{-i(\lambda,\alpha_0)}\Gamma(i(\lambda,\alpha_0))}{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2} m_\alpha + 1+ i(\lambda,\alpha_0)\right)\right) \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{1}{2}m_\alpha + m_{2\alpha} + i(\lambda,\alpha_0)\right)\right)},</math>
where
<math display="block">c_0 = 2^{m_\alpha/2 + m_{2\alpha}} \Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2} (m_\alpha+m_{2\alpha} +1)\right).</math>

The general [[Gindikin–Karpelevich formula]] for '''c'''(λ) is an immediate consequence of this formula and the multiplicative properties of '''c'''<sub>''s''</sub>(λ).

==Paley–Wiener theorem==
The Paley-Wiener theorem generalizes the [[Paley-Wiener theorem|classical Paley-Wiener theorem]] by characterizing the spherical transforms of smooth ''K''-bivariant functions of compact support on ''G''. It is a necessary and sufficient condition that the spherical transform be ''W''-invariant and that there is an ''R'' > 0 such that for each ''N'' there is an estimate

<math display="block">|\tilde{f}(\lambda)|\le C_N (1+|\lambda|)^{-N} e^{R \left|\operatorname{Im} \lambda\right|}.</math>

In this case ''f'' is supported in the closed ball of radius ''R'' about the origin in ''G''/''K''.

This was proved by Helgason and Gangolli ({{harvtxt|Helgason|1970}} pg. 37).

The theorem was later proved by {{harvtxt|Flensted-Jensen|1986}} independently of the spherical inversion theorem, using a modification of his method of reduction to the complex case.<ref>The second statement on supports follows from Flensted-Jensen's proof by using the explicit methods associated with
[[Kostant polynomial]]s instead of the results of Mustapha Rais.</ref>

==Rosenberg's proof of inversion formula==
{{harvtxt|Rosenberg|1977}} noticed that the Paley-Wiener theorem and the spherical inversion theorem could be proved simultaneously, by a trick which considerably simplified previous proofs.

The first step of his proof consists in showing directly that the inverse transform, defined using Harish-Chandra's '''c'''-function, defines a function supported in the closed ball of radius ''R'' about the origin if the Paley-Wiener estimate is satisfied. This follows
because the integrand defining the inverse transform extends to a meromorphic function on the [[complexification]] of <math>\mathfrak{a}^*</math>; the integral can be shifted to <math>\mathfrak{a}^* + i\mu t</math> for μ in <math>\mathfrak{a}^*_+</math> and ''t'' > 0. Using Harish-Chandra's expansion
of φ<sub>λ</sub> and the formulas for '''c'''(λ) in terms of [[Gamma function]]s, the integral can be bounded for ''t'' large and hence can be shown to vanish outside the closed ball of radius ''R'' about the origin.<ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|pages=452–453}}</ref>

This part of the Paley-Wiener theorem shows that
<math display="block"> T(f)=\int_{\mathfrak{a}_+^*} \tilde{f}(\lambda) |c(\lambda)|^{-2} \, d\lambda</math>
defines a distribution on ''G''/''K'' with support at the origin ''o''. A further estimate for the integral shows that it is in fact given by a measure and that therefore there is a constant ''C'' such that
<math display="block">  T(f) = Cf(o).</math>

By applying this result to
<math display="block">f_1(g)=\int_K f(x^{-1}kg)\, dk,</math>
it follows that
<math display="block"> Cf=\int_{\mathfrak{a}_+^*} \tilde{f}(\lambda) \varphi_\lambda |c(\lambda)|^{-2} \, d\lambda.</math>

A further scaling argument allows the inequality ''C'' = ''1'' to be deduced from the Plancherel theorem and Paley-Wiener theorem on <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Rosenberg|1977}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=588–589}}</ref>

==Schwartz functions==
The Harish-Chandra Schwartz space can be defined as<ref>{{harvnb|Anker|1991|page=347}}</ref>

<math display="block">\mathcal{S}(K\backslash G/K)= \left \{f\in C^\infty(G/K)^K:\sup_{x} \left |(1+d(x,o))^m (\Delta + I)^n f(x) \right |<\infty \right \}.</math>

Under the spherical transform it is mapped onto <math>\mathcal{S}(\mathfrak{a}^*)^W,</math> the space of ''W''-invariant
[[Schwartz function]]s on <math>\mathfrak{a}^*.</math>

The original proof of Harish-Chandra was a long argument by induction.<ref name="HarishChandra1958" /><ref name="HarishChandra1958a" /><ref>{{harvnb|Helgason|1984|page=489}}</ref> {{harvtxt|Anker|1991}} found a short and simple proof, allowing the result to be deduced directly from versions of the Paley-Wiener and spherical inversion formula. He proved that the spherical transform of a Harish-Chandra Schwartz function is a classical Schwartz function. His key observation was then to show that the inverse transform was continuous on the Paley-Wiener space endowed with classical Schwartz space [[seminorm]]s, using classical estimates.
